I'm not gonna lie: there are multiple issues with Cathedral and some that aren't even visible but would come up eventually.

The point of this whole thing is to just let the mind fly as far and as high as it can. Reality will filter out bullshit. It always does.

Osage orange is a consideration for all the reasons you mentioned and more. Reality of USDA zone etc. will effectively filter what could go in the system depending on where it is. For instance, when I picked black walnut I didn't ever mean to say "Only black walnut works in this". There are many different configurations possible and all of them would have to be guided by where the system is. As far as wind breaks are concerned each tree row adds to the overall windbreaking for the entire system. It'll protect the animals and trap snow in winter (if it's somewhere that gets snow).

The economics, build, timelines and people are all serious issues and I'm not dismissing any of them. The fact is that this whole thing keeps developing in my head and it won't stop.

As far as the grazing thing it all depends on rainfall, soil quality and effective photosynthesis (driven in part by proper nutrient in the soil etc.). If there isn't enough recovery, which is what my base assumption is, in a year then putting animals back on is begging for desertification. If there IS enough recovery then HELL YES! Put them bad boys back on. I'd love to get 3-5 full passes (more if humanly possible). I come from West Texas so I'm just assuming "drought" and worst case scenario.

If you haven't heard the more in-depth podcasts I've done on this please see https://www.bitcoinandshow.com/tag/cathedral/

I'm not dismissing anything you have said here and this is exactly the kind of pushback I was hoping Cathedral would drum up so keep doing it. But also Cathedral is an idea: What would you do? What would you change? What would make it work in your environment? 

There is so much more we could talk about but dirty dishes await. My Signal is NunyaBidness.01 if you want to get a hold of me there.

After three years of growing beautiful tomato seedlings from seed I’ve finally recognized that regardless of pot size, tomatoes in open ground or very deep beds open to the earth will always outperform those in pots. They need way more legroom and temperature moderation in the root zone then even a very large pot can provide. Plus I’m certain that the actual connection to the Earth is part of the equation. ￼ In year one, I got 80 pounds of tomatoes off seven plants that all reached almost 6 feet in height, in an open-bottomed 8’x4’ bed that currently holds my cucumber and squash trellises. This year the only tomato plant that is thriving is the one whose roots are free to go anywhere they like. ￼The ones in pots, even very large 5 gallon containers, are visibly stressed the same as the ones in 3 gallon pots were last year. At first I thought it was a soil problem, but I’ve done everything right in that regard in these pots and they just don’t like it. ￼ when these black pots get irradiated by sun all day, the temperature in the root zone can easily reach 80°F and it’s amazing how quickly they become root bound. I will still get some yield off of these but their big brother in the bed is going to put them to shame. ￼

It’s all part of the process of working out the kinks in a small setting so that when we move to a space with some serious production capability, I’ll have figured many of these things out. On Sunday we are going to look at a nearly 6 acre partially forested place with animal corrals, fencing around the perimeter and loads of growing space. ￼Lord willing, we will be building our vision for self sufficiency there. 

I just love growing things and doing these experiments a year at a time. ￼#gardenstr #homesteading
